source_review.notes: Checked every cited primary source live. Four Kimball Group pages, two Microsoft dimensional-modeling pages, Google Cloud's current BigQuery nested-field guidance, and current PostgreSQL EXPLAIN and constraint documentation each returned HTTP 200. Star, snowflake, flattened-dimension, semantic-model, nested-data, plan and key claims are scoped to those sources.

evidence: Reviewed schema graph S=(V,E), fact/dimension node sets, edge tuple, match degree d_e(a), functional-dependency chain and flattened-dimension relational expression.
Checked base-key projection, hierarchy attribute sets, query population, additive partition equation and workload-cost function arguments.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Notation keeps logical cardinality and semantic time premises separate from observed platform cost.

evidence: Executed schema-shape-equivalence with Python 3.14.4 and reproduced 3 fact rows, 3 flat product rows and 8 total normalized hierarchy rows.
Independently recomputed Technology as 100+50=150 and Food as 80 through both paths.
Confirmed exact base product key equality, complete hierarchy references and identical sorted aggregate maps.
The first run exposed and corrected an expected snowflake row count of 7 to the actual 3+3+2=8.
numerical_recomputation.notes: All values are deterministic exact integers; row counts describe only the synthetic fixture and do not imply storage or runtime cost.

evidence: Re-derived that d_e(a)=1 for every governed child makes one hierarchy join emit exactly one pair per child.
Checked induction over a chain of strict total many-to-one edges to preserve one row and one base key per D0 member.
Verified additive rollup equality requires hierarchy groups to be exhaustive and mutually exclusive; a many-to-many bridge violates that partition without allocation or primary membership.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: Losslessness proves key/row preservation under stated edge premises, not attribute truth, temporal compatibility or performance.

evidence: Reviewed zero, one and multiple parent matches; orphan, null and special members; duplicate parent keys; cycles and conflicting redundant paths.
Reviewed current versus as-of hierarchy, overlapping effective intervals, late dimension members and changed organization labels.
Reviewed fixed-depth, ragged, variable-depth and genuine many-to-many hierarchies with bridge/allocation behavior.
Reviewed role-playing dimensions, bidirectional filters, security paths, nested UNNEST fanout, fact-to-fact joins and stale serving copies.
Reviewed scale, skew, cold/warm cache, concurrency, scan/shuffle, compression and engine-version benchmark boundaries.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Each adversary is tied to a rejection, special-member, bridge, path, history or benchmark control.

evidence: Traced fact grain, unique resolution, coverage, temporal compatibility, hierarchy ownership, path clarity, conformance, row preservation, measure preservation and reproducibility through the sixteen-step mechanism.
Checked all ten worked examples for a declared edge/cardinality failure and corresponding durable model control.
Confirmed that canonical and serving shapes remain distinct and that every performance recommendation retains correctness gates.
invariant_checking.notes: The chapter never treats schema appearance, aggregate coincidence or optimizer behavior as a substitute for key-set and match-degree evidence.

evidence: Verified the one-edge base case and the hierarchy-chain induction step for exact one-match resolution.
Confirmed projection retains the base key and assumes no duplicate base keys, so it cannot collapse distinct governed members.
Checked the explicit caveat that row preservation alone does not prove time or attribute correctness.
proof_review.notes: The argument is sufficient for the named row-preservation claim and does not overclaim query equivalence outside compatible filters, time and measures.

evidence: The induction is explicitly labeled 'Proof sketch — strict many-to-one hierarchy flattening preserves base rows.'
Other equations are definitions or conditional invariants and are not presented as externally verified theorems.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Formal scope and missing premises are visible adjacent to the proof.

evidence: The executable fixture is labeled as a constrained exact-integer equivalence demonstration, not optimizer or production evidence.
Platform performance discussion repeatedly requires controlled workload measurements and does not claim a universal winner.
Worked scenarios are synthetic and benchmark criteria are prescriptions, not reported experimental results.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No production prevalence, cost, latency or causal performance result is asserted.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed star, snowflake, one-big-table, operational normalization, flattened hierarchy, bridge, outrigger, role-playing and conformed-dimension distinctions. The chapter correctly makes process, grain, cardinality and time prior to physical shape.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed keys, special members, hierarchy ownership, security paths, constraints, reconciliation, query-plan evidence, workload benchmarking, serving derivatives, monitoring and bidirectional migration. The design workflow produces implementable tables, tests and acceptance evidence.

pedagogical_review.notes: The module moves from the two canonical shapes through lossless joins, exceptions and platform choices. The compact fixture makes equivalence inspectable; ten examples cover practical failures; five exercises progress from basic design through bridges, conformance, benchmarking and zero-downtime migration with complete answers.

limitations: Internal evidence record only. No external academic, Kimball Group, Microsoft, Google Cloud, PostgreSQL, data-warehouse practitioner, security, cost or production review is claimed. The in-memory fixture does not measure database constraints, optimizer quality, storage compression, network shuffle, concurrency, access control or workload-specific economics.
